newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan opposition to set up new government.
newsitem.headline: Afghan opposition to set up new government.

text.p: Factions opposed to Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban movement said on Friday they planned to form a new provisional government.

Abdul Rahim Ghafoorzai, deputy foreign minister in the ousted government led by then-president Burhanuddin Rabbani, told a news conference the new administration would be formed mainly of technocrats rather than guerrilla faction leaders.
"I can assure you that the new government will mainly consist of non-party members," Ghafoorzai said in the northern opposition-held city of Mazar-i-Sharif.
He said the previous administration, driven from Kabul by the Taleban last September, had failed to bring peace.
"In Kabul one of the main problems was a lack of adequately qualified intellectual members of the government who had the ability to bring about a substantial change," he added.
He said he hoped to announce the members of the new government within two days.

A declaration adopted by the newly-formed United Islamic and National Front for the Salvation of Afghanistan on Thursday said a provisional national council would be convened until a loya jirga, or traditional grand council, could be convened.
The provisional council, including scholars, tribal, spiritual and national leaders and technocrats based inside or outside Afghanistan, would serve as a provisional parliament.
The declaration said the government would have to convene a loya jirga within six to nine months under the supervision of the United Nations and the Organisation of Islamic Conference.
One of the loya jirga's tasks would be to set a date for free and fair elections in Afghanistan, the declaration added.
Ghafoorzai said the Taleban's recent defeats in northeastern Afghanistan might make them more willing to negotiate.
"The Taleban's recent failure to bring the whole country under their rule is one of the most important reasons for us to believe that they might follow the path of peace and dialogue," he said.
The Taleban, bent on imposing strict Islamic rule across Afghanistan, has suffered a series of military setbacks at the hands of opposition forces in the last three weeks.
They briefly occupied Mazar-i-Sharif last month but were driven from the city with heavy losses. They lost the town of Pul-i-Khumri, their last foothold in the north, on Wednesday.
The opposition declaration called on Pakistan to use its influence to end the conflict.

"The United Front calls on Pakistan to end its antagonistic policy towards the Islamic state (the opposition) and people of Afghanistan and declare its readiness for direct negotiations to establish fraternal and normal relations with Afghanistan.
"Instead of supporting one side in the conflict, the government of Pakistan is expected, to play a positive and effective role for the cessation of the conflict," it said.
Pakistan denies opposition charges that it favours the Taleban, saying it is neutral in the Afghan conflict.
